2179.dloc: Phonology, 'Syllable structure' p. 63 and 'Word structure' p. 64; 'Rhythm groups' pp. 65-66
2179.prule: No word-stress rule. Accent is a lexically contrastive suprasegmental with four types (level = stressed + high level pitch; falling = pitch downglide with diminishing stress, long nuclei only; breathy; glottal) versus unaccented; stress is a correlate of accent, not an independent culminative feature. Level accent occurs in any position of the word and more than one syllable of a word may be accented (čámá 'tomorrow', gášé 'white'); the initial syllable is accented in an overwhelming majority of words; glottal accent is rarely non-initial; falling and breathy accents are never word-final.
2179.srule: Not mentioned in Davis 1964, Phonology pp. 59-66 (accent pp. 63-64, Word structure p. 64, Rhythm groups pp. 65-66): accents are lexical and unranked, a word may carry more than one.

2179.exq_: Although any syllable of the word may be unaccented, the initial syllable is accented in an overwhelming majority of the words. (p. 64; a statistical tendency, not a rule; the source states no positional stress rule to which exceptions could attach)
2179.tone: Davis's 'accent' is a four-way contrastive category defined by pitch contour and phonation (level/falling/breathy/glottal) against unaccented; stress is stated as a correlate: 'Level accented vowels are stressed and normally have a high level pitch' (p. 63); falling accent shows 'a downglide in pitch together with diminishing stress'; the breathy accent's 'initial voiced segment is short and stressed, and has a relatively high pitch'; 'Terminal glottal closure is written as a segmental feature only in unstressed syllables'. Pitch on level-accented vowels is conditioned by word position and preceding consonant. Accent is non-culminative (two accented vowels in čámá 'tomorrow'). Phrase-level: one syllable per rhythm group receives 'extra intensive stress', most often the group-initial syllable, with declining pitch and intensity thereafter (pp. 65-66). Morphophonemics (pp. 66 ff.) describe accent-type alternations (glottal -> level after glottalized pronominal prefixes).

2180.prule: Main stress (Hauptton) is concentrated on the root syllable (Wurzelsilbe) of the word; prefixes for-, bə-, jə- and other pretonic syllables are unstressed ('vortonige Nebensilben'); derivational suffixes are unstressed or bear a strong or weak secondary stress. Loanwords keep a non-initial stress (koléndər, fomīləc, popīr, stakít, šakét; tsījəretta, akkərāt, lokəmotīfə, komfərmatsjuon), and the suffix -haftəc has drawn main stress onto itself (wāráftəc 'wahrhaftig'). Position is set by morpheme class (root vs affix), not by syllable count or weight.
2180.srule: Non-root syllables are either unstressed or carry a strong or weak Nebenton (secondary stress), placed by morpheme, not by rhythm: Nebenton lies on full-vowel derivational suffixes (-hāit, -šop, -nis, -zām, -bār, -uŋə; also arbāit, hābuk, nītīc), strong Nebenton on the third syllable of obscured compounds (forrəmədāx 'Vormittag', nommədāx, šāulərbāit) and on -ēr after l/n (dreslēr, klempnēr); mnd. -ig/-isch/-inge (> -əc/-əš/-əjə) have lost Nebenton and -lic has hardly any; prefixes for-, bə-, jə- are unstressed. No alternating/rhythmic secondary stress is described (Hille 1939 §§102-104).

2181.dq: Sec. 1.5.1.1 p.35: 'Word-final accent is shared by all QG languages. ... There are exceptions in the QG languages. In Eastern Yugur some word structures trigger changes in the position of the accent.' Fn.207 p.174: 'Junast (1981:14) only mentions the basic rule that accent is word-final.' The rule in 3.14.5 is stated over stems in citation form; fn.208 gives suffixed word forms.
2181.dloc: Sec. 3.14.5 'Accent-related lengthening in non-final syllables', pp.174-175 incl. fn.207-209; basic rule sec. 2.4.3 'Accent placement' p.63; also sec. 1.5.1.1 'Final accent and consequences' p.35 and the 'Accent' paragraph p.86.
2181.heavy: 'a contraction length or diphthong' (long vowel or diphthong) 'will take the accent (vowel height is irrelevant)'; second tier among short vowels: a short non-high vowel outranks ə (< short high vowels), i.e. 'the accent tends to avoid the vowel ə... if a non-high vowel is also present in the stem'. Codas are not part of the rule; p.174 notes only that in the affected EYu words the first syllable 'may either be open or closed'.
2181.dflt: Final syllable when all vowels are short and of one height class (al'tan, hele'ɣen, pə'čəg, xəmə'sən) or when the final syllable has a short non-high vowel; if the final syllable has ə and a non-high vowel exists, the rightmost non-high vowel (first syllable in disyllables: 'ġatən; rightmost available in longer stems: he'nesən, 'belwəsən).
2181.prule: Word accent is final by default (al'tan, hele'ɣen, pə'čəg, xəmə'sən). If the stem contains a long (contraction-length) vowel or diphthong, that syllable takes the accent wherever it is ('ki:re, 'ǰe:ren vs du'la:n, ǰɔ'rɔ:); with several long vowels, the last one. In stems of short vowels only, the accent avoids ə (the reflex of the four short high vowels in non-first syllables) when a non-high vowel is present: disyllables with final ə accent the first syllable ('ġatən, 'xɔ:nə); trisyllabic and longer stems accent the rightmost non-high vowel (he'nesən, 'belwəsən, ǰə'ğasən, xulă'ğaičə). Sec. 2.4.3: accent 'normally falls on the last syllable... although predictable deviations occur under some phonetic circumstances'; p.86: 'accent placement in Eastern Yugur is more complicated, and partly correlated with vowel length'.

2184.prule: Lexical (phonemic) stress: stress marking is part of the underlying representation of each root and of some affixes, is not predictable from other phonological properties, and yields minimal pairs. Surface primary stress is confined to a right-edge two-syllable window (ultimate or penultimate syllable of the prosodic word), exactly one primary stress per prosodic word.
2184.srule: At most one secondary stress per prosodic word, not obligatory and not confined to the final two-syllable window; it realises an underlying stress mark on a syllable that does not get the primary stress: stress-marked prefixes (/bà-/ 'smelling of' vs /ba-/ acquisition, /bàujáŋ/ vs /baujáŋ/; /nà-/) and a stress-marked root syllable displaced to antepenultimate position by suffixation (/túlbu-i/ -> [tùl.bu.í]). No rhythmic/alternating secondary stress is described.
2184.quote: It is necessary to include stress marking in an account of Eastern Tawbuid phonology since stress is contrastive in this language. Stress does not fall regularly on a particular syllable of the prosodic word, and it cannot be reliably predicted from other phonological properties of a word. Rather, stress is part of the underlying phonological representation of a word, and minimal pairs of words differentiated only by stress exist. Some examples are given here. 2186.prule: None. 2186.tone: No lexical tone and no pitch accent. 2190.prule: Fixed initial stress: the main stress is always on the first syllable of the radical (stem), which is the first syllable of the orthographic word because the preposed particles (TAM/person proclitics, articles) are unstressed and written as separate words; syllable weight plays no role. tn.quote: El otomí es un idioma tonal, es decir, cada sílaba se pronuncia ya sea en tono bajo (`) o tono alto (´), y las combinaciones de estos dos: alto-bajo o descendente (^), o bajo-alto o ascendente (ˇ). … Una raíz puede llevar tono alto, bajo, o la combinación de ellos, pero las partículas que se le anteponen (proclíticos) llevan sólo tono alto o bajo y nunca las combinaciones de ellos. … Hay que tener mucho cuidado de no confundir el tono con el acento. El acento no se escribe en otomí. El tono es el nivel musical en que se pronuncia la sílaba.
tn.translation: Otomi is a tonal language, that is, each syllable is pronounced either in low tone (`) or high tone (´), and the combinations of these two: high-low or falling (^), or low-high or rising (ˇ). ... A root can carry high tone, low tone, or the combination of them, but the particles placed before it (proclitics) carry only high or low tone and never their combinations. ... One must take great care not to confuse tone with stress. Stress is not written in Otomi. Tone is the musical level at which the syllable is pronounced.

2191.prule: Two-tone (H/L) system 'with both a lexical and syntactic basis'; no lexical minimal pairs by tone; no word-stress rule is stated in the reachable pages (the word 'stress' does not occur in them). Every nominal has a lexically specified 'basic tone' identified on its penultimate vowel; H is confined to the final two syllables of the root: H penult implies H final (HH), L penult implies H final (LH), so only the penult needs underlying marking. Verbs are inherently L and acquire a fixed H only from particular inflections (jussive: H on the first syllable; negative imperative: H on the penult). Placement is only partly predictable from shape (CVCa with short -a -> LH; -aa-final nominals 'overwhelmingly' L penult; long non-low final vowel 'overwhelmingly' H penult; almost all long-vowel suffixes induce H on the preceding syllable); a root H made antepenultimate by suffixation 'must shift to low', the suffix's own tone supplying the word-final H (xeesúmmáa LHH -> xeesumm-óotá LLHH). Surface tone further alternates by syntactic context (basic tone vs all-low vs predicate-nominal pattern, 2.3).

2197.prule: No word-stress rule is stated by any reachable source. The one trained fieldworker (Schebesta 1952, own 1949-50 data) transcribes Efe with a four-way tone key (ton haut, ton chanté, ton haut ascendant, ton retombant) and shows tone doing grammatical work in Efe (plural marked by high tone when the suffix -eni fuses with the final vowel; elision/contraction leaves traces in 'la hauteur du ton musical'). 2202.dq: When, after collecting noun items, these were examined to ascertain what tonal patterns occur on the nouns, it was found that, tonetically, the following occurred: Low - low (LL), Low - mid (LM), Mid - low (ML), Mid - mid (MM), Mid - high (MH), High - mid (HM); low-high (LH) and High-low (HL) and high-high (HH) did not occur.

2202.tone: Both sources treat the entire suprasegmental system as tone: three level tonemes H, M, L (1973 pp. 293-295; 1989 p. 98), with the two-tones-plus-downstep alternative discussed and rejected, and the system called 'probably in a fluid transitory stage'. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the Ehuẹun chapter of the 1973 thesis (scan pp. 277-296), in the 1973 general tone section (pp. 88-93 scan), or anywhere in the 1989 book ('accented' once, about Yoruba spoken as a second language, p. 12). No claim about word stress is made either way.

tn.quote: The tones of Ehueun do not submit easily to analysis. The whole system is probably in a fluid transitory stage. The tonetic facts will be presented briefly below as a first step to examining the system in terms of two possible analyses: a 'two tones plus downstep' analysis, end a ‘three level tones' analysis. ... If this analysis be adopted, then Ehugun has high, mid, and low tonemes at the tonemic level. ... Even so, the latter analysis is adopted ... It could be suggested that this is a system ... in transition between a two tones plus downstep system and a three level tone system.
